profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting between two collaborators preparing a comparative review article and invited workshop session titled "Revisiting implementation theory" for an interdisciplinary policy-and-practice conference. The project compares how urban planning research and healthcare implementation research conceptualize implementation, with the immediate agenda focused on deciding what the first synthesis package will include, how the literature will be divided between them, what counts as the initial comparison matrix, and when the "Friday draft" and "framework table" are due. The expected outcome is an agreed work plan for producing an outline, a shared evidence table, and a draft set of cross-domain comparison sections.

members.name: Dr. Leila Hart
members.role: Urban Planning Associate Professor and lead convenor
members.expertise: Planning theory, policy implementation, governance, and comparative urban research
members.background: Leads a small urban governance lab and has published on planning theory history, especially 1960s-1980s implementation debates and contemporary planning practice.
members.private_state: Wants the piece to re-establish urban planning as theoretically sophisticated rather than merely borrowing from healthcare; is worried about overcommitting before a heavy teaching week and wants a credible conference-ready package quickly.
hidden_assumptions: A "framework table" means a concise analytic matrix of major conceptual traditions and representative frameworks, not a comprehensive inventory of every implementation model mentioned in the literature.

The "core literature" in planning is the canon of implementation-focused planning scholarship plus a limited set of recent meta-level papers, so screening peripheral practice-evaluation papers is unnecessary for the first pass.
A "Friday draft" means a polished internal working draft circulated by end of day Friday in her local time zone, suitable for the two of them to revise over the weekend.

When they say "implementation outcomes," they are using the phrase loosely to refer to whether implementation is explained at all in a field's theory, not specifically to the healthcare outcomes taxonomy.
If they "split healthcare and planning," each person is primarily responsible for their home domain but will only note obvious crossover concepts rather than fully coding the other field.

members.name: Dr. Aaron Velez
members.role: Health Services Research Fellow and co-author
members.expertise: Implementation science, evidence synthesis, and translational healthcare frameworks
members.background: Works in a medical school implementation lab, routinely produces structured reviews and framework mappings for clinical and public health audiences.
members.private_state: Wants the article to be legible to implementation-science reviewers and to demonstrate methodological rigor; is concerned the planning side may look impressionistic unless the comparison uses explicit synthesis conventions.
hidden_assumptions: A "framework table" means a near-exhaustive evidence map listing named frameworks, constructs, level of analysis, empirical use, and citation details in spreadsheet form.

The "core literature" means all records meeting the agreed concept boundaries after database searching and screening, including adjacent service-delivery and community-health planning papers if they address implementation.
A "Friday draft" means something deposited in the shared drive by 11:59 PM UTC on Friday, even if rough, so he can batch-process and annotate it over the weekend.
The phrase "implementation outcomes" refers to the established implementation-science family of outcomes such as adoption, fidelity, penetration, sustainability, and acceptability.
If they "split healthcare and planning," both domains should still be coded using the same extraction template so the synthesis is directly comparable from the start.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to produce a "framework table" before drafting.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks this is a compact manuscript-ready comparison table with perhaps 10-15 major frameworks or conceptual traditions and short interpretive notes.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks this is a detailed evidence-mapping spreadsheet capturing most named frameworks encountered, with standardized fields for constructs, setting, and usage.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are accustomed to using the phrase "framework table" as obvious research shorthand, and because both versions are indeed tables about frameworks, the difference in granularity feels too mundane to clarify.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the core literature
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to start with the "core literature" in each field.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the canonical planning implementation debate plus a bounded set of theory-focused review and agenda-setting papers, excluding many applied delivery studies.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the full set of eligible literature after structured searching, including neighboring implementation-relevant studies if they fit the concept.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase "core literature" sounds like a sensible narrowing device and each assumes the other shares their field's implicit convention for what is naturally central versus peripheral.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss whether to include "implementation outcomes" in the comparison matrix.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 uses the phrase generically to mean any way a paper characterizes whether implementation happened, was explained, or produced downstream practice effects.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 interprets it as the specific implementation-science taxonomy of outcomes and expects those categories to appear explicitly in extraction and comparison.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The term is highly familiar in healthcare and intuitively legible in ordinary language, so M1 sees no reason to flag her looser usage while M2 assumes the technical meaning is shared.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the first draft will be ready "by Friday."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes "by Friday" means a clean internal draft by around 5 PM her local time, with missing references and formatting mostly resolved.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes "by Friday" means any workable draft uploaded before midnight UTC, even if still rough, as long as he can start coding comments.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Deadline talk in collaborative academic meetings often uses casual shorthand, and both think they are being flexible and cooperative rather than discussing something requiring formal specification.

The angle has to show that planning already has theoretical depth on implementation, not just that we can borrow healthcare terminology. If we can get a clean synthesis structure in place fast, I can shape the argument and have something respectable for the workshop.
